changed.was: Albert Bacon Blanton (1881 to 1959) was born on a farm near the Frankfort distillery and joined it in 1897, at sixteen, as an office boy. He rose to run it as president from 1921, and after the repeal of Prohibition he had Warehouse H built in metal, quick to raise, in 1935. When he entertained important guests, the story goes, he drew whiskey for them from chosen barrels in the centre of that warehouse. Elmer T. Lee (1919 to 2013), then master distiller, remembered that habit, and in 1984, near the end of his career, he launched a bourbon bottled one barrel at a time and named it for the colonel: Blanton's Single Barrel, which the distillery calls the first modern single barrel bourbon. Each bottle carries its barrel number and the day the barrel was emptied, written by hand, and its stopper is one of eight horse and jockey figures, each marked with one letter of the name. The distillery took the name Buffalo Trace in 1999. Behind a bar Blanton's is the bottle that taught guests to ask for a single barrel, and the proof that no two barrels read quite alike.
changed.now: Albert Bacon Blanton (1881 to 1959) was born on a farm near the Frankfort distillery and joined it in 1897, at sixteen, as an office boy. He rose to be its president in 1921 and led it until 1952; after the repeal of Prohibition he had Warehouse H built in metal, quick to raise, in 1935. When he entertained important guests, the story goes, he drew whiskey for them from chosen barrels in the centre of that warehouse. Elmer T. Lee (1919 to 2013), then master distiller, remembered that habit, and in 1984, near the end of his career, he launched a bourbon bottled one barrel at a time and named it for the colonel: Blanton's Single Barrel, which the distillery calls the first single barrel bourbon. Each bottle carries its barrel number and the day the barrel was emptied, written by hand, under a horse and jockey stopper; since 1999 there have been eight of them, each marked with one letter of the name. changed.was: Seagram introduced Eagle Rare in 1975 as a ten year old Kentucky straight bourbon at 101 proof, made, by most accounts, at its Four Roses distillery in Lawrenceburg. The Sazerac Company bought the label from Seagram in 1989, and in 1992 bought the Frankfort distillery that it renamed Buffalo Trace in 1999, where the bourbon is made. In 2005 the strength came down to 90 proof and the bottling was sold as a single barrel bourbon, each bottle drawn from one barrel. About 2012, by the accounts of the time, a new automated bottling line came into use; because it can let a little of one barrel run into the next, the words Single Barrel came off the label, and the bottle was redesigned with the age statement moved to the back. The distillery describes every barrel as chosen with care, and the whiskey kept its recipe and its ten years. For a bartender it is the lesson in reading a label as it stands: ten years of oak and one recipe, with no claim to a single barrel.

changed.was: Booker Noe (1929 to 2004), a grandson of Jim Beam, was the family distillery's master distiller when he created Knob Creek in 1992. It was one of the Small Batch Bourbon Collection, four bourbons beside Booker's, Baker's and Basil Hayden's, and he built it, by the producer's account, on the bonded whiskey of the years before Prohibition, the kind the Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897 stood behind: long in oak and bottled at 100 proof. The name is a place, not a person. Knob Creek is the stream that ran by the Kentucky farm where Abraham Lincoln (1809 to 1865) spent his boyhood, a farm his family knew as the Knob Creek place. In late 2016 the producer took the nine year statement off the label, saying it could not promise that every barrel had reached nine years, and in 2020 the statement came back. For a bartender Knob Creek is a steady 100 proof bourbon for the stirred drinks, and a plain lesson that the words small batch say nothing of age: the number on the label does.

changed.was: Elijah Craig (died 1808) was a Baptist minister from Virginia who settled in Kentucky, where, as the house tells it, he set up a distillery in 1789 on Elkhorn Creek, at what became Georgetown. The claim that he invented bourbon, or first charred his barrels, goes back to a history of Kentucky published in 1874, and historians treat it as legend. Heaven Hill of Bardstown chose his name for a new label in 1986: a twelve year old small batch bourbon. Fire destroyed the Bardstown distillery in 1996, and from 1999 the house distilled at Bernheim in Louisville while its whiskey went on ageing around Bardstown. To stretch its stock of older barrels as the label grew, Heaven Hill took the twelve year statement off the back label in 2016, and the Small Batch became a mingling of barrels of eight to twelve years at the same 94 proof. For a bartender it is the bottle that shows what long years in oak bring to a small batch bourbon, with a founding story to tell as the legend it is.

Fire destroyed the Bardstown distillery in 1996, and from 1999 the house distilled at Bernheim in Louisville while its whiskey went on ageing around Bardstown. To stretch its stock of older barrels as the label grew, Heaven Hill took the twelve year statement off the back label in 2016, and the Small Batch became a mingling of barrels of eight to twelve years at the same 94 proof. For a bartender it is the bottle that shows what long years in oak bring to a small batch bourbon, with a founding story to tell as the legend it is.

changed.was: Russell's Reserve began as a son's tribute to his father, master distiller of the Wild Turkey Distillery at Lawrenceburg. By the brand's account, his son made a small batch bourbon in 1998 to mark his father's forty-five years at the distillery, and called it Russell's Reserve. The label came to market in 2001 as a ten year old Kentucky straight bourbon at 101 proof, the strength of the house's flagship, and in 2005 the ten year old was brought down to 90 proof. In March 2013 came Russell's Reserve Single Barrel, each bottle from one barrel, bottled at 110 proof and without chill filtering. The son was named master distiller beside his father in 2015, and the brand credits the two with choosing its barrels. Behind a bar it shows the Wild Turkey style at its plainest: deep char, a low barrel entry, one cask at a time, and the strength left high.
